title: Πῦρ ἀκάματον
about: Athena gives Diomedes, the son of Tydeus, force and courage, and makes fire blaze from his helmet and shield like the late-summer star, then sends him into the thickest of the fighting. Two sons of Dares, Hephaestus’ priest among the Trojans, come out against him: Phegeus throws and misses, Diomedes does not, and Hephaestus hides the other, Idaeus, in night so that the old man is not wholly grieved. Athena then leads Ares out of the battle to sit by the Scamander, and the Danaans turn the Trojans back, each leader killing his man. Agamemnon, Idomeneus, Menelaus, Meriones, Meges and Eurypylus each kill a Trojan in turn, and the poet gives each victim a short history. Diomedes rages across the plain like a river in winter spate that no bridge or fence can hold, and the Trojan lines break before him. Lycaon’s son draws his bow and hits him in the right shoulder, and cries out in triumph; but Diomedes is not brought down, and he steps back to the chariot and asks Sthenelus to draw the arrow out.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ αὖ Τυδεΐδῃ Διομήδεϊ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη
δῶκε μένος καὶ θάρσος, ἵν’ ἔκδηλος μετὰ πᾶσιν
Ἀργείοισι γένοιτο ἰδὲ κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἄροιτο·
sentences.i: Then Pallas Athena gave the son of Tydeus, Diomedes, force and courage, so that he might stand out plainly among all the Argives and win a good name;
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ αὖ ‘then again’ opens a new scene, and Athena is the subject: Τυδεΐδῃ Διομήδεϊ are two datives, ‘to Tydeus’-son Diomedes’, and δῶκε is an unaugmented past (Attic ἔδωκε) governing μένος καὶ θάρσος ‘force and courage’. Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη ‘Pallas Athena’ is a stock name, and the meaning of Παλλάς is disputed. ἵνα with the optatives γένοιτο and ἄροιτο gives purpose after a past verb, ‘so that he might become … and win’. ἔκδηλος is a rare word for ‘plain to see’, and ἄροιτο is the aorist optative middle of αἴρομαι ‘carry off, win’. κλέος ἐσθλόν is ‘good fame’, a good name among men.

sentences.t:
δαῖέ οἱ ἐκ κόρυθός τε καὶ ἀσπίδος ἀκάματον πῦρ
ἀστέρ’ ὀπωρινῷ ἐναλίγκιον, ὅς τε μάλιστα
λαμπρὸν παμφαίνῃσι λελουμένος ὠκεανοῖο·
sentences.i: She kindled an untiring fire for him from his helmet and shield, like the star of late summer that shines most brightly when it has bathed in Oceanus;
sentences.n: δαῖε is ‘kindled’ (δαίω, unaugmented past; Athena is still the subject), with οἱ ‘for him’ and ἐκ κόρυθος τε καὶ ἀσπίδος ‘from helmet and shield’. ἀκάματον ‘untiring’ is ἀ- + κάμνω ‘tire’. ἀστέρ’ is the dative ἀστέρι with its ι elided, the thing the fire is ἐναλίγκιον ‘like’, and ὀπωρινῷ ‘of late summer’ comes from ὀπώρη, the season at summer’s end when fruit ripens; the Greek does not name the star. ὅς τε is the epic τε of a general truth, and παμφαίνῃσι is a subjunctive with the ending -σι (= παμφαίνῃ) ‘shines all-bright’, with λαμπρόν as an adverb ‘brightly’. λελουμένος is the perfect middle participle of λούω, ‘having bathed’, and ὠκεανοῖο is the genitive of Ὠκεανός, the great stream the heavenly bodies rise from.

sentences.t:
τοῖόν οἱ πῦρ δαῖεν ἀπὸ κρατός τε καὶ ὤμων,
ὦρσε δέ μιν κατὰ μέσσον ὅθι πλεῖστοι κλονέοντο.
sentences.l:
Such a fire she kindled for him from head and shoulders,
and roused him into the middle, where most were being thrown into confusion.
sentences.i: Such a fire she kindled for him from his head and shoulders, and sent him into the middle of the fighting, where the most men were being thrown into confusion.
sentences.n: τοῖον … πῦρ is ‘such a fire’, picking up the comparison; δαῖεν is another unaugmented past, ‘she kindled’. ὦρσε is the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse, set in motion’ (the verb of ὄρνυτο below) with μιν ‘him’, and κατὰ μέσσον is ‘into the middle’. ὅθι is ‘where’, πλεῖστοι ‘most (men)’, and κλονέοντο is the passive of κλονέω ‘drive in confusion’, ‘were being thrown into confusion’.

sentences.t:
ἦν δέ τις ἐν Τρώεσσι Δάρης ἀφνειὸς ἀμύμων
ἱρεὺς Ἡφαίστοιο· δύω δέ οἱ υἱέες ἤστην
Φηγεὺς Ἰδαῖός τε μάχης εὖ εἰδότε πάσης.
sentences.l:
There was among the Trojans a certain Dares, rich, blameless,
priest of Hephaestus; and two sons of his were there,
Phegeus and Idaeus, well knowing all fighting.
sentences.i: Among the Trojans there was a certain Dares, a rich and blameless man, priest of Hephaestus, who had two sons, Phegeus and Idaeus, both well skilled in every kind of fighting.
sentences.n: ἦν δέ τις ‘there was a certain’ introduces a new man, Δάρης ‘Dares’, ἀφνειός ‘rich’ and ἀμύμων ‘blameless’; ἀμύμων is a stock epithet whose real meaning is not known, and it is kept as ‘blameless’ even where it tells us nothing. ἱρεύς is Ionic for ἱερεύς ‘priest’, and Ἡφαίστοιο the genitive of Ἥφαιστος. οἱ is ‘to him’, a dative of possession with ἤστην (the dual imperfect of εἰμί, ‘the two were’), so ‘two sons were his’. Φηγεύς and Ἰδαῖος are named after υἱέες ‘sons’, and εἰδότε is the dual participle of οἶδα ‘knowing’, agreeing with them; μάχης … πάσης is the genitive of what they know, ‘all fighting’.

sentences.t:
τώ οἱ ἀποκρινθέντε ἐναντίω ὁρμηθήτην·
τὼ μὲν ἀφ’ ἵπποιιν, ὃ δ’ ἀπὸ χθονὸς ὄρνυτο πεζός.
sentences.l:
Those two, having drawn apart, set out facing him;
the two from the horses, and he from the ground rushed on, on foot.
sentences.i: These two drew apart and set out to face him, the pair from their horses, and he rushing up from the ground, on foot.
sentences.n: The dual is used for the two brothers throughout: τώ ‘those two’ (the article as a pronoun), ἀποκρινθέντε ‘having separated themselves’, ἐναντίω ‘facing’ and ὁρμηθήτην ‘set out’ are all dual forms, and οἱ is ‘him’, Diomedes, who is not named in the lines. τὼ μὲν … ὃ δέ sets the two against the one: ἀφ’ ἵπποιιν is ‘from the (pair of) horses’, a dual dative-genitive form that stands for the chariot they ride, while ὃ δ’ ‘he’ is Diomedes, who ὄρνυτο ‘rushed on’ (the imperfect middle of ὄρνυμι) ἀπὸ χθονός ‘from the ground’, πεζός ‘on foot’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦσαν ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντες
Φηγεύς ῥα πρότερος προΐει δολιχόσκιον ἔγχος·
sentences.l:
And when they were near, going against one another,
Phegeus first sent forth his long-shadowed spear;
sentences.i: And when they were near, advancing on one another, Phegeus was first to send forth his long-shadowed spear;
sentences.n: Line 14 is the same line as 3.15, where the two armies close on each other, and its English is kept. Φηγεύς ῥα πρότερος is ‘Phegeus first’ (ῥα is the particle ἄρα), and προΐει is the imperfect of προΐημι ‘send forth’. δολιχόσκιον ‘long-shadowed’ is δολιχός ‘long’ + σκιά ‘shadow’, the usual sense; ἔγχος is ‘spear’, as it is wherever it stands.

sentences.t:
Τυδεΐδεω δ’ ὑπὲρ ὦμον ἀριστερὸν ἤλυθ’ ἀκωκὴ
ἔγχεος, οὐδ’ ἔβαλ’ αὐτόν·
sentences.l:
and over Tydeus’-son’s left shoulder went the point
of the spear, and he did not hit him;
sentences.i: and the point of the spear went over the left shoulder of the son of Tydeus, and did not hit him;
sentences.n: The sentence turns on ἤλυθ’ ἀκωκή, ‘the point went’ (ἤλυθε is the epic aorist of ἔρχομαι, Attic ἦλθε, and ἀκωκή is the ‘point’ of the spear, ἔγχεος in the next line). Τυδεΐδεω is the epic genitive -εω of Τυδεΐδης (Attic Τυδεΐδου); ὑπὲρ ὦμον ἀριστερόν is ‘over the left shoulder’. οὐδ’ ἔβαλ’ αὐτόν is ‘and did not hit him himself’: the spear flew past the man.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ὕστερος ὄρνυτο χαλκῷ
Τυδεΐδης·
sentences.l:
and he, later, rushed on with the bronze,
Tydeus’-son;
sentences.i: and then the son of Tydeus rushed on with the bronze;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is ‘and he’ (the article as a pronoun), and the name Τυδεΐδης comes last, in apposition; ὕστερος is ‘later, second’. ὄρνυτο χαλκῷ ‘rushed on with the bronze’ is the same phrase as at 3.349–350, where δεύτερον ‘in second place’ stands for ὕστερος; χαλκῷ is the dative of the weapon, the bronze-tipped spear.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ οὐχ ἅλιον βέλος ἔκφυγε χειρός,
ἀλλ’ ἔβαλε στῆθος μεταμάζιον, ὦσε δ’ ἀφ’ ἵππων.
sentences.l:
and from his hand the shaft did not escape in vain,
but he hit him on the chest, between the nipples, and thrust him from the horses.
sentences.i: and his shaft did not leave his hand in vain, but struck the man in the chest between the nipples and thrust him from his horses.
sentences.n: τοῦ δ’ … χειρός is ‘from his hand’, a genitive of separation, with οὐχ ἅλιον ‘not vain’ agreeing with βέλος ‘shaft’ and ἔκφυγε ‘escaped’ (unaugmented). ἔβαλε στῆθος is ‘he hit (him) on the chest’, the chest as the part struck, and μεταμάζιον ‘between the nipples’ comes from μετά + μαζός ‘breast’. ὦσε is ‘thrust’ (ὠθέω), and ἀφ’ ἵππων ‘from the horses’ again means the chariot team that Phegeus was riding.

sentences.t:
Ἰδαῖος δ’ ἀπόρουσε λιπὼν περικαλλέα δίφρον,
οὐδ’ ἔτλη περιβῆναι ἀδελφειοῦ κταμένοιο·
sentences.l:
But Idaeus sprang away, leaving the very fair chariot,
and did not dare to stand over his brother, slain;
sentences.i: But Idaeus leapt away, leaving the very fair chariot, and did not dare to stand over his slain brother;
sentences.n: Ἰδαῖος is the second brother, now named as the subject; ἀπόρουσε is the aorist of ἀπορούω ‘spring away’ and λιπών the aorist participle of λείπω ‘leaving’. περικαλλής is ‘very fair’ (περι- ‘very’), and δίφρος is the ‘chariot’. ἔτλη is the aorist of τλάω ‘dare, endure’, and περιβῆναι with the genitive ἀδελφειοῦ κταμένοιο is ‘to stride over his slain brother’ to protect the body; ἀδελφειοῦ is ‘brother’, and κταμένοιο the aorist middle participle of κτείνω, used as a passive, ‘slain’.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδέ κεν αὐτὸς ὑπέκφυγε κῆρα μέλαιναν,
ἀλλ’ Ἥφαιστος ἔρυτο, σάωσε δὲ νυκτὶ καλύψας,
ὡς δή οἱ μὴ πάγχυ γέρων ἀκαχήμενος εἴη.
sentences.i: For not even he himself would have escaped the black spirit of death; but Hephaestus guarded him and saved him by covering him in night, so that the old man should not be altogether grieved.
sentences.n: γάρ explains why Idaeus left his brother: οὐδὲ … οὐδέ κεν ‘for not even would he’ followed by κεν with an aorist indicative (ὑπέκφυγε) is a past unreal, ‘would have escaped’. κῆρα μέλαιναν is ‘the black death-fate’, the κήρ that brings death. ἔρυτο is ‘guarded’ (a past of ἔρυμαι, ‘protect’) and σάωσε ‘saved’ (= ἔσωσε), with νυκτὶ καλύψας ‘having covered him in night’. Ἥφαιστος is the god whose priest Dares is, in line 10. ὡς with the optative εἴη gives purpose, γέρων ‘old man’ is Dares, and ἀκαχήμενος is a perfect middle participle, ‘grieved’; οἱ is a dative of interest, ‘for him’, and the Greek does not say whom it points to, so it is left unspoken in English.

sentences.t:
ἵππους δ’ ἐξελάσας μεγαθύμου Τυδέος υἱὸς
δῶκεν ἑταίροισιν κατάγειν κοίλας ἐπὶ νῆας.
sentences.l:
And the horses, having driven them out, the son of great-hearted Tydeus
gave to his companions to take down to the hollow ships.
sentences.i: And the son of great-hearted Tydeus drove the horses out and gave them to his companions to take down to the hollow ships.
sentences.n: ἐξελάσας ‘having driven out’ is the aorist participle of ἐξελαύνω, and ἵππους, the captured horses, is its object, placed first for emphasis; Τυδέος υἱός is ‘the son of Tydeus’, Diomedes unnamed, with the stock epithet μεγάθυμος ‘great-hearted’. δῶκεν is ‘gave’ with the dative ἑταίροισιν ‘to his companions’, and κατάγειν ‘to lead down’ is an infinitive of purpose; κοίλας … νῆας is ‘the hollow ships’, the Achaean ships drawn up on the shore.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες δὲ μεγάθυμοι ἐπεὶ ἴδον υἷε Δάρητος
τὸν μὲν ἀλευάμενον, τὸν δὲ κτάμενον παρ’ ὄχεσφι,
πᾶσιν ὀρίνθη θυμός·
sentences.i: And when the great-hearted Trojans saw the two sons of Dares, the one having got away and the other lying slain beside the chariot, the spirit was stirred in all of them;
sentences.n: ἴδον is an unaugmented aorist (Attic εἶδον), and υἷε is the dual accusative ‘the two sons’. τὸν μὲν … τὸν δέ are ‘the one … the other’: ἀλευάμενον is the aorist middle participle of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’ (here: escape death), and κτάμενον ‘slain’ is the participle of κτείνω seen at line 21. παρ’ ὄχεσφι is ‘beside the chariot’, with the ending -φι. πᾶσιν ὀρίνθη θυμός is ‘in all the spirit was stirred’, ὀρίνθη being the passive aorist of ὀρίνω ‘stir, agitate’.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη
χειρὸς ἑλοῦσ’ ἐπέεσσι προσηύδα θοῦρον Ἄρηα·
sentences.l:
but gleaming-eyed Athena,
taking him by the hand, addressed him with words, impetuous Ares:
sentences.i: but gleaming-eyed Athena took impetuous Ares by the hand and spoke to him:
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘but’ turns to the gods, and Athena’s stock epithet γλαυκῶπις is ‘gleaming-eyed’. χειρὸς ἑλοῦσα is ‘taking him by the hand’ (the aorist participle of αἱρέω, with the genitive of the part held), ἐπέεσσι is the epic dative plural ‘with words’, and προσηύδα is ‘was addressing’ (the imperfect of προσαυδάω). θοῦρος is ‘impetuous’, an epithet of Ἄρης that comes from θρῴσκω ‘leap’ (the exact sense is not certain), and Ἄρηα is the accusative of Ἄρης.

sentences.t:
Ἆρες Ἄρες βροτολοιγὲ μιαιφόνε τειχεσιπλῆτα
οὐκ ἂν δὴ Τρῶας μὲν ἐάσαιμεν καὶ Ἀχαιοὺς
μάρνασθ’, ὁπποτέροισι πατὴρ Ζεὺς κῦδος ὀρέξῃ,
νῶϊ δὲ χαζώμεσθα, Διὸς δ’ ἀλεώμεθα μῆνιν;
sentences.l:
“Ares, Ares, mortal-ruining, blood-stained, wall-stormer,
shall we not now let the Trojans and the Achaeans
fight, to whichever of the two father Zeus may grant glory,
and we two draw back, and avoid the wrath of Zeus?”
sentences.i: “Ares, Ares, ruin of mortals, blood-stained, stormer of walls, shall we not now let the Trojans and the Achaeans fight, to whichever of them father Zeus may grant glory, while we two draw back and avoid the wrath of Zeus?”
sentences.n: This is a speech: Athena speaks to Ares and asks a question. Ἆρες Ἄρες is a doubled vocative, followed by three epithets: βροτολοιγέ ‘mortal-ruining’ (βροτός ‘mortal’ + λοιγός ‘ruin’), μιαιφόνε ‘blood-stained’ (μιαίνω ‘stain’ + φόνος ‘slaughter’) and τειχεσιπλῆτα ‘wall-stormer’, whose second element is disputed. οὐκ ἂν δὴ … ἐάσαιμεν is ‘shall we not let’, an optative with ἄν used as a polite suggestion, with the infinitive μάρνασθ’ ‘fight’; ὁπποτέροισι is ‘to whichever of the two’, ὀρέξῃ ‘may grant’ (the subjunctive of ὀρέγω ‘stretch out’), κῦδος ‘glory’. νῶϊ is the dual ‘we two’, and χαζώμεσθα ‘draw back’ and ἀλεώμεθα ‘avoid’ are subjunctives (the vowel is long, ω) continuing the question, ‘and we two draw back and avoid …?’; Διὸς … μῆνιν is ‘the wrath of Zeus’.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰποῦσα μάχης ἐξήγαγε θοῦρον Ἄρηα·
sentences.l: So having spoken, she led out of the fighting impetuous Ares;
sentences.i: So she spoke, and led impetuous Ares out of the fighting;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰποῦσα ‘so having spoken’ is the formula that closes a speech (the feminine aorist participle of εἶπον). μάχης is a genitive of separation, ‘out of the fighting’, and ἐξήγαγε is the aorist of ἐξάγω ‘lead out’. Athena has taken Ares by the hand, so he goes with her.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἔπειτα καθεῖσεν ἐπ’ ἠϊόεντι Σκαμάνδρῳ,
Τρῶας δ’ ἔκλιναν Δαναοί·
sentences.l:
him then she seated on high-banked Scamander,
and the Trojans the Danaans turned back;
sentences.i: She then seated him on the high-banked Scamander, and the Danaans turned the Trojans back;
sentences.n: τὸν μὲν ἔπειτα is ‘him then’, Ares; καθεῖσεν is the aorist of καθίζω ‘seat’, and ἐπ’ … Σκαμάνδρῳ ‘on the Scamander’ is the river by the plain. ἠϊόεντι is a rare epithet built on ἠϊών ‘bank, shore’; ‘high-banked’ is the usual sense, and it is not certain. In Τρῶας δ’ ἔκλιναν Δαναοί the object comes first and the subject last: ἔκλιναν is the aorist of κλίνω ‘bend, turn’, here ‘turn back’, so the Danaans turn the Trojans.

sentences.t:
ἕλε δ’ ἄνδρα ἕκαστος
ἡγεμόνων·
sentences.l:
and took a man each
of the leaders;
sentences.i: and each of the leaders killed his man;
sentences.n: ἕλε is the unaugmented aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’, here ‘kill’, and ἕκαστος ‘each’ is the subject, with ἡγεμόνων ‘of the leaders’ as a genitive of the whole; ἄνδρα is ‘a man’. The lines after this name the leaders one by one, beginning with Agamemnon.

sentences.t:
πρῶτος δὲ ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων
ἀρχὸν Ἁλιζώνων Ὀδίον μέγαν ἔκβαλε δίφρου·
sentences.l:
and first, lord of men Agamemnon
the commander of the Halizones, great Odius, threw from his chariot;
sentences.i: and first Agamemnon, lord of men, threw great Odius, the commander of the Halizones, from his chariot;
sentences.n: πρῶτος is ‘first’, and ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is Agamemnon’s stock title. ἀρχόν ‘commander’ is in apposition to Ὀδίον μέγαν ‘great Odius’, and together they are the one object of ἔκβαλε, with Ἁλιζώνων the genitive plural of the people he leads; δίφρου is a genitive of separation, ‘out of the chariot’.

sentences.t:
πρώτῳ γὰρ στρεφθέντι μεταφρένῳ ἐν δόρυ πῆξεν
ὤμων μεσσηγύς, διὰ δὲ στήθεσφιν ἔλασσε,
δούπησεν δὲ πεσών, ἀράβησε δὲ τεύχε’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ.
sentences.i: For in the back of the man who turned first he fixed his spear, between the shoulders, and drove it through his chest; and he fell with a thud, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.n: Agamemnon is the subject of πῆξεν ‘fixed’ and ἔλασσε ‘drove’, and Odius is the man who falls (πεσών); πρώτῳ στρεφθέντι is a dative participle phrase, ‘for him, first to turn’, with μεταφρένῳ ‘in the back’ and δόρυ ‘spear’. ὤμων μεσσηγύς is ‘between the shoulders’ and διὰ δὲ στήθεσφιν ἔλασσε ‘and drove it through the chest’, with the ending -φιν; line 41 is the same as 57 below except that 57 ends ἔλασσεν with the movable ν (line 57 is also Odyssey 22.93), and the English is kept. Line 42 is the same as 4.504, and its English is kept: δούπησεν is ‘fell with a thud’, and ἀράβησε ‘clattered’ is of the armour.

sentences.t:
Ἰδομενεὺς δ’ ἄρα Φαῖστον ἐνήρατο Μῄονος υἱὸν
Βώρου, ὃς ἐκ Τάρνης ἐριβώλακος εἰληλούθει.
sentences.l:
And Idomeneus slew Phaestus, the son of the Maeonian
Borus, who from rich-soiled Tarne had come.
sentences.i: And Idomeneus killed Phaestus, the son of the Maeonian Borus, who had come from rich-soiled Tarne.
sentences.n: ἐνήρατο is the aorist middle of ἐναίρω ‘kill, slay’, with Ἰδομενεύς as subject and Φαῖστον as object. Μῄονος υἱὸν Βώρου is read as ‘son of Borus the Maeonian’: Μῄονος is the genitive of Μῄων, a man of Maeonia in Asia Minor, and it agrees with Βώρου across υἱόν. ὃς … εἰληλούθει is the pluperfect of ἔρχομαι, ‘had come’, from Τάρνη, a place named only here, with ἐριβώλακος ‘rich-soiled’, the same as the Odyssey’s word.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἄρ’ Ἰδομενεὺς δουρικλυτὸς ἔγχεϊ μακρῷ
νύξ’ ἵππων ἐπιβησόμενον κατὰ δεξιὸν ὦμον·
sentences.l:
Him then Idomeneus, famed-for-the-spear, with his long spear
stabbed, as he was about to mount the horses, in the right shoulder;
sentences.i: Idomeneus, famed for his spear, stabbed him with his long spear in the right shoulder as he was about to mount his horses;
sentences.n: τὸν μὲν ἄρ’ is ‘him then’, and Ἰδομενεὺς δουρικλυτός is ‘Idomeneus, famed-for-the-spear’ (δόρυ ‘spear’ + κλυτός ‘famous’). νύξ’ is the unaugmented aorist of νύσσω ‘prick, stab’, and ἔγχεϊ μακρῷ is the dative ‘with a long spear’. ἵππων ἐπιβησόμενον is the future participle ‘about to mount the horses’, the horses being the chariot, and κατὰ δεξιὸν ὦμον is ‘in the right shoulder’.

sentences.t: ἤριπε δ’ ἐξ ὀχέων, στυγερὸς δ’ ἄρα μιν σκότος εἷλε.
sentences.l: and he crashed down from the chariot, and hateful darkness took him.
sentences.i: and he crashed down from his chariot, and hateful darkness took him.
sentences.n: ἤριπε is ‘crashed down’ (the aorist of ἐρείπω), and ἐξ ὀχέων is ‘out of the chariot’, with the plural ὄχεα for the one vehicle. στυγερὸς σκότος is ‘hateful darkness’ (στυγερός ‘hateful’), the darkness of death, and εἷλε is ‘took’, the aorist of αἱρέω with μιν ‘him’.

sentences.t: τὸν μὲν ἄρ’ Ἰδομενῆος ἐσύλευον θεράποντες·
sentences.l: Him then Idomeneus’ attendants were stripping;
sentences.i: Idomeneus’ attendants stripped him of his armour;
sentences.n: τὸν μὲν ἄρ’ is ‘him, then’, the same words that began line 45: this is Idomeneus’ own victim, Phaestus, and not his men. ἐσύλευον is the imperfect of συλεύω ‘strip (of arms)’, and Ἰδομενῆος is the epic genitive of Ἰδομενεύς; θεράποντες is ‘attendants’.

sentences.t:
υἱὸν δὲ Στροφίοιο Σκαμάνδριον αἵμονα θήρης
Ἀτρεΐδης Μενέλαος ἕλ’ ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι
ἐσθλὸν θηρητῆρα·
sentences.i: And Menelaus, the son of Atreus, killed Scamandrius, the son of Strophius, a man skilled in the hunt, with his sharp spear, a good hunter;
sentences.n: The object stands first: υἱὸν … Στροφίοιο Σκαμάνδριον is ‘Scamandrius, the son of Strophius’, and Ἀτρεΐδης Μενέλαος ‘Atreus’-son Menelaus’ is the subject. ἕλ’ is ἕλε, ‘took’ in the sense ‘killed’; ἔγχεϊ ὀξυόεντι is the dative ‘with a sharp spear’ (ὀξυόεις ‘pointed’). αἵμονα θήρης is ‘skilled in the hunt’ (αἵμων ‘skilled’, with the genitive), and ἐσθλὸν θηρητῆρα ‘a good hunter’ is in apposition; ἐσθλός is ‘good’ at the thing it is said of.

sentences.t:
δίδαξε γὰρ Ἄρτεμις αὐτὴ
βάλλειν ἄγρια πάντα, τά τε τρέφει οὔρεσιν ὕλη·
sentences.l:
for Artemis herself taught him
to strike all wild things, which the forest feeds on the mountains;
sentences.i: for Artemis herself had taught him to strike every wild creature that the forest feeds in the mountains;
sentences.n: δίδαξε is the unaugmented aorist of διδάσκω ‘taught’, with Ἄρτεμις αὐτή ‘Artemis herself’ as the subject, and βάλλειν ‘to strike’ is what he was taught. ἄγρια πάντα is ‘all wild things’, and τά τε τρέφει is a relative clause with the epic τε of a general truth, ‘which (as a rule) the forest feeds’; ὕλη is ‘forest’, and οὔρεσιν is the epic dative plural, ‘on the mountains’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὔ οἱ τότε γε χραῖσμ’ Ἄρτεμις ἰοχέαιρα,
οὐδὲ ἑκηβολίαι ᾗσιν τὸ πρίν γε κέκαστο·
sentences.l:
but then did not help him Artemis, the arrow-pourer,
nor the far-shooting skills in which before he had excelled;
sentences.i: but at that time Artemis, who showers her arrows, did not help him, nor did his far-shooting skills, in which he had excelled before;
sentences.n: ἀλλά sets the next line against the one before: οὔ οἱ … χραῖσμ’ is ‘did not help him’ (χραῖσμ’ is the aorist ἔχραισμε of χραισμέω ‘avail’, with οἱ ‘him’), and its subjects are Ἄρτεμις ἰοχέαιρα and ἑκηβολίαι ‘far-shooting skills’. ἰοχέαιρα is ‘who showers her arrows’ (ἰός ‘arrow’ + a second element taken either from χέω ‘pour’ or from χαίρω ‘delight in’; the house rendering takes χέω). ᾗσιν is the relative, dative plural, ‘in which’, and κέκαστο is the pluperfect of καίνυμαι, ‘had excelled’; τὸ πρίν γε is ‘before’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μιν Ἀτρεΐδης δουρικλειτὸς Μενέλαος
πρόσθεν ἕθεν φεύγοντα μετάφρενον οὔτασε δουρὶ
ὤμων μεσσηγύς, διὰ δὲ στήθεσφιν ἔλασσεν,
ἤριπε δὲ πρηνής, ἀράβησε δὲ τεύχε’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ.
sentences.l:
but him Atreus’-son, Menelaus famed-for-the-spear,
before himself as he fled wounded in the back with a spear,
between the shoulders, and through the chest he drove it;
and he crashed down headlong, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.i: But Menelaus, the son of Atreus, famed for his spear, wounded him in the back with a spear as he fled before him, between the shoulders, and drove it through his chest; and he crashed down headlong, and his armour clattered upon him.
sentences.n: ἀλλά μιν is ‘but him’, and Ἀτρεΐδης δουρικλειτὸς Μενέλαος ‘Atreus’-son, Menelaus famed-for-the-spear’ is the subject: δουρικλειτός is the Ionic-epic form of δουρικλυτός. πρόσθεν ἕθεν φεύγοντα is ‘fleeing before himself’, ἕθεν being the reflexive ‘himself’ (Menelaus), and μετάφρενον is ‘the back’, as the part wounded (οὔτασε, ‘wounded’). Line 57 is the same as Odyssey 22.93 and its English is kept, and the second half of line 58, ἀράβησε δὲ τεύχε’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ, is the end of line 42, with ἤριπε δὲ πρηνής ‘and he crashed down headlong’ before it.

sentences.t:
Μηριόνης δὲ Φέρεκλον ἐνήρατο, τέκτονος υἱὸν
Ἁρμονίδεω, ὃς χερσὶν ἐπίστατο δαίδαλα πάντα
τεύχειν·
sentences.i: And Meriones killed Phereclus, the son of the builder Harmonides, who knew how to make every kind of intricate work with his hands;
sentences.n: Μηριόνης is the subject and Φέρεκλον the object of ἐνήρατο ‘slew’ (as at line 43). τέκτονος υἱὸν Ἁρμονίδεω is ‘the son of the builder Harmonides’: τέκτων covers carpenter and builder, a worker in wood, and Ἁρμονίδεω is the epic genitive -εω; the relative ὅς is Phereclus himself, who ἐπίστατο ‘knew how’ (with the infinitive τεύχειν, in the next line, ‘to make’). δαίδαλα πάντα is ‘all intricate works’, and χερσίν is the epic dative plural ‘with his hands’.

sentences.t: ἔξοχα γάρ μιν ἐφίλατο Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη·
sentences.l: for above all others loved him Pallas Athena;
sentences.i: for Pallas Athena loved him above all others;
sentences.n: The γάρ clause explains why the skill is mentioned: ἔξοχα is ‘above all, pre-eminently’ as an adverb, and ἐφίλατο is the aorist middle of φιλέω ‘love’, with μιν ‘him’; the subject is Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη ‘Pallas Athena’, who is the goddess of crafts.

sentences.t:
ὃς καὶ Ἀλεξάνδρῳ τεκτήνατο νῆας ἐΐσας
ἀρχεκάκους, αἳ πᾶσι κακὸν Τρώεσσι γένοντο
οἷ τ’ αὐτῷ, ἐπεὶ οὔ τι θεῶν ἐκ θέσφατα ᾔδη.
sentences.l:
who also for Alexander built the well-balanced ships,
evil-beginning, which to all the Trojans became an evil
and to himself, since he knew nothing of the prophecies from the gods.
sentences.i: He it was who also built for Alexander the well-balanced ships that began the evil, which became a bane to all the Trojans and to himself, since he knew nothing of the prophecies from the gods.
sentences.n: ὃς καί is ‘who also’, with τεκτήνατο ‘built’ (the aorist middle of τεκταίνομαι, from τέκτων); Ἀλεξάνδρῳ is the dative ‘for Alexander’, the Trojan prince also named Paris. νῆας ἐΐσας is ‘well-balanced ships’, a stock phrase whose sense is not certain, and ἀρχεκάκους ‘evil-beginning’ (ἀρχή ‘beginning’ + κακός ‘evil’) agrees with it. αἳ … γένοντο is ‘which became’ (unaugmented), κακόν ‘an evil’ the predicate, and οἷ τ’ αὐτῷ is ‘and to himself’, the reflexive οἷ, which points back to Phereclus (the next clause is about his ignorance), not to Alexander. ᾔδη is the pluperfect of οἶδα, ‘he knew’, with θεῶν ἐκ θέσφατα ‘the prophecies from the gods’, ἐκ placed after its noun θεῶν.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν Μηριόνης ὅτε δὴ κατέμαρπτε διώκων
βεβλήκει γλουτὸν κατὰ δεξιόν·
sentences.l:
Him, when Meriones was overtaking him, pursuing,
he had struck on the right buttock;
sentences.i: When Meriones, giving chase, overtook him, he struck him on the right buttock;
sentences.n: τὸν μὲν … ὅτε δή is ‘him … when’, with the ὅτε clause first: κατέμαρπτε is the imperfect of καταμάρπτω ‘overtake’ (‘was overtaking’) and διώκων ‘pursuing’. βεβλήκει is a pluperfect, ‘had struck’, but it is used as a plain past; γλουτόν is ‘the buttock’, and κατὰ δεξιόν ‘on the right (side)’.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ διαπρὸ
ἀντικρὺ κατὰ κύστιν ὑπ’ ὀστέον ἤλυθ’ ἀκωκή·
sentences.l:
and the point right through,
straight through the bladder, below the bone, went;
sentences.i: and the point went clean through, straight through the bladder, below the bone;
sentences.n: ἣ δέ is ‘and it’, the feminine article agreeing with ἀκωκή ‘point’, which comes last in the line below; ἤλυθ’ is the epic aorist ἤλυθε, Attic ἦλθε, ‘went’. διαπρό ‘right through’ and ἀντικρύ ‘straight through’ are adverbs, and κατὰ κύστιν ὑπ’ ὀστέον is ‘through the bladder, below the bone’ (κύστις ‘bladder’, ὀστέον ‘bone’), the bone of the hip.

sentences.t: γνὺξ δ’ ἔριπ’ οἰμώξας, θάνατος δέ μιν ἀμφεκάλυψε.
sentences.l: and on his knees he crashed down, wailing, and death enfolded him.
sentences.i: and he crashed down on his knees, wailing, and death enfolded him.
sentences.n: γνύξ is ‘on the knees’, an adverb, and ἔριπ’ is the unaugmented ἔριπε of ἐρείπω ‘crash down’. οἰμώξας is the aorist participle of οἰμώζω ‘wail’, and θάνατος δέ μιν ἀμφεκάλυψε is ‘and death enfolded him’ (the aorist of ἀμφικαλύπτω, ‘cover about’), with μιν ‘him’.

sentences.t:
Πήδαιον δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπεφνε Μέγης Ἀντήνορος υἱὸν
ὅς ῥα νόθος μὲν ἔην, πύκα δ’ ἔτρεφε δῖα Θεανὼ
ἶσα φίλοισι τέκεσσι χαριζομένη πόσεϊ ᾧ.
sentences.l:
And Pedaeus Meges slew, Antenor’s son,
who indeed was illegitimate, but carefully reared him heavenly Theano
equally with her dear children, gratifying her husband.
sentences.i: Meges killed Pedaeus, the son of Antenor, who was illegitimate, though heavenly Theano brought him up carefully, treating him as she did her dear children, to please her husband.
sentences.n: Read the accusative first: Πήδαιον … Ἀντήνορος υἱόν is the victim, ‘Pedaeus, Antenor’s son’, and Μέγης ‘Meges’ is the killer (ἔπεφνε, ‘slew’, an aorist of the same root as φόνος). ὅς ῥα νόθος μὲν ἔην is ‘who indeed was illegitimate’ (ἔην is the epic ἦν), and δέ answers it: πύκα δ’ ἔτρεφε δῖα Θεανώ, ‘but heavenly Theano reared him carefully’, ἔτρεφε being the imperfect of τρέφω. ἶσα φίλοισι τέκεσσι is ‘equally with her dear children’, and χαριζομένη πόσεϊ ᾧ ‘gratifying her husband’, where ᾧ is the possessive ‘her own’ and πόσεϊ the dative of πόσις.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν Φυλεΐδης δουρὶ κλυτὸς ἐγγύθεν ἐλθὼν
βεβλήκει κεφαλῆς κατὰ ἰνίον ὀξέϊ δουρί·
sentences.l:
Him Phyleus’-son, famous with the spear, having come close,
had struck on the nape of the head with the sharp spear;
sentences.i: The son of Phyleus, famous with the spear, came close and struck him on the nape of the head with his sharp spear;
sentences.n: Φυλεΐδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Phyleus’, and it stands for Meges, the killer already named in line 69. δουρὶ κλυτός is ‘famous with the spear’, and ἐγγύθεν ἐλθών ‘having come close’ is the aorist participle of ἔρχομαι. βεβλήκει is a pluperfect used as a plain past, ‘had struck’; κεφαλῆς κατὰ ἰνίον is ‘on the nape (the sinews at the back) of the head’, and ὀξέϊ δουρί ‘with the sharp spear’.

sentences.t: ἀντικρὺ δ’ ἀν’ ὀδόντας ὑπὸ γλῶσσαν τάμε χαλκός·
sentences.l: and straight up through the teeth, under the tongue, cut the bronze;
sentences.i: and the bronze cut straight up through his teeth, under the tongue;
sentences.n: ἀντικρύ ‘straight through’ and ἀν’ ὀδόντας ‘up through the teeth’ show the track of the blade upward from the nape, and ὑπὸ γλῶσσαν is ‘under the tongue’. τάμε is the unaugmented aorist of τέμνω ‘cut’, and χαλκός is ‘bronze’ by metonymy for the spear-point.

sentences.t: ἤριπε δ’ ἐν κονίῃ, ψυχρὸν δ’ ἕλε χαλκὸν ὀδοῦσιν.
sentences.l: and he crashed down in the dust, and the cold bronze took with his teeth.
sentences.i: and he crashed down in the dust, taking the cold bronze in his teeth.
sentences.n: ἤριπε is ‘crashed down’ and ἐν κονίῃ ‘in the dust’ (κονίῃ is a dative in -ῃ). ἕλε is the unaugmented aorist ‘took (hold of)’, and ὀδοῦσιν is the dative plural of ὀδούς ‘tooth’, ‘with his teeth’; ψυχρὸν χαλκόν is ‘the cold bronze’.

sentences.t:
Εὐρύπυλος δ’ Εὐαιμονίδης Ὑψήνορα δῖον
υἱὸν ὑπερθύμου Δολοπίονος, ὅς ῥα Σκαμάνδρου
ἀρητὴρ ἐτέτυκτο, θεὸς δ’ ὣς τίετο δήμῳ,
sentences.l:
And Eurypylus, Euaemon’s-son — heavenly Hypsenor,
son of high-spirited Dolopion, who of Scamander
had been made praying-priest, and like a god was honoured in the land —
sentences.i: Eurypylus, the son of Euaemon — heavenly Hypsenor, the son of high-spirited Dolopion, who had been made priest of Scamander and was honoured like a god in the land —
sentences.n: The sentence is not finished: Εὐρύπυλος is the subject and Ὑψήνορα δῖον ‘heavenly Hypsenor’ the object, but the verb does not come until ἔλασ’ in line 80, after a fresh start with τὸν μὲν ἄρ’. Εὐαιμονίδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Euaemon’, and ὑπερθύμου ‘high-spirited’ is Dolopion’s stock epithet. ὅς ῥα is ‘who indeed’, ἀρητήρ ‘praying-priest’ (the one who makes prayers) is ‘priest’, and ἐτέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω, ‘had been made’; Σκαμάνδρου is ‘of Scamander’, the river-god. θεὸς δ’ ὣς τίετο δήμῳ is ‘and was honoured like a god in the land’, the same words as Odyssey 14.205, of a man honoured among the Cretans.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἄρ’ Εὐρύπυλος, Εὐαίμονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός,
πρόσθεν ἕθεν φεύγοντα μεταδρομάδην ἔλασ’ ὦμον
φασγάνῳ ἀΐξας, ἀπὸ δ’ ἔξεσε χεῖρα βαρεῖαν·
sentences.i: Eurypylus, Euaemon’s splendid son, struck him on the shoulder with his sword as he fled before him, rushing after him at a run, and hewed off his heavy hand;
sentences.n: τὸν μὲν ἄρ’ resumes Hypsenor after the long introduction, and Εὐρύπυλος Εὐαίμονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός ‘Eurypylus, Euaemon’s splendid son’ is the subject; the same words end 2.736, in the Catalogue of Ships. ἔλασ’ is ‘struck’ (ἐλαύνω, ‘drive’), with ὦμον the part struck, and πρόσθεν ἕθεν φεύγοντα is ‘fleeing before himself’, as at line 56. μεταδρομάδην is ‘at a run after (him)’, and ἀΐξας ‘darting’, the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω. ἔξεσε is the aorist of ξέω ‘scrape, hew’, which with ἀπό (ἀπὸ δ’ … ἔξεσε, the preverb apart) is ‘hew off’, and χεῖρα βαρεῖαν ‘the heavy hand’. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the last syllable of Εὐρύπυλος is short but stands in a long place, at the main caesura before the vowel of Εὐαίμονος.

sentences.t:
αἱματόεσσα δὲ χεὶρ πεδίῳ πέσε· τὸν δὲ κατ’ ὄσσε
ἔλλαβε πορφύρεος θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα κραταιή.
sentences.l:
and the bloody hand fell on the plain; and him, down over the eyes,
seized purple death and strong fate.
sentences.i: and the bloody hand fell on the plain; and purple death and strong fate seized him, down over his eyes.
sentences.n: αἱματόεσσα is ‘bloody’ (αἷμα ‘blood’), and πεδίῳ πέσε is ‘fell on the plain’. τὸν δὲ κατ’ ὄσσε is ‘and him down over the eyes’, ὄσσε being the dual ‘two eyes’, and ἔλλαβε is the aorist of λαμβάνω with a doubled λ, ‘seized’. πορφύρεος ‘purple’ is a colour word of wide range, dark and gleaming, and ‘purple’ is kept; μοῖρα κραταιή is ‘strong fate’, with κραταιή the same as κρατερή ‘strong’.

sentences.t: ὣς οἳ μὲν πονέοντο κατὰ κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην·
sentences.l: So these were toiling in strong battle;
sentences.i: So these men were toiling in strong battle;
sentences.n: ὣς οἳ μὲν marks the end of a series of single kills: οἳ is ‘these’, and πονέοντο is the uncontracted imperfect middle of πονέω ‘toil’. κατὰ κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην is ‘in strong battle’, the stock phrase, with ὑσμίνη ‘battle’.

sentences.t:
Τυδεΐδην δ’ οὐκ ἂν γνοίης ποτέροισι μετείη
ἠὲ μετὰ Τρώεσσιν ὁμιλέοι ἦ μετ’ Ἀχαιοῖς.
sentences.l:
But Tydeus’-son you could not tell among which of the two he was,
whether he mingled with the Trojans or was among the Achaeans.
sentences.i: But you could not tell which side the son of Tydeus was on, whether he was mingling with the Trojans or was among the Achaeans.
sentences.n: οὐκ ἂν γνοίης is ‘you could not know’, an optative with ἄν, and ‘you’ is any onlooker; the object Τυδεΐδην is placed first. ποτέροισι μετείη is an indirect question, ‘among which of the two he was’ (ποτέροισι is dative plural ‘which of the two’, μετείη the optative of μέτειμι ‘be among’), and ἠέ … ἦ ‘whether … or’ gives the two sides, with ὁμιλέοι the optative of ὁμιλέω ‘mix with’.

sentences.t:
θῦνε γὰρ ἂμ πεδίον ποταμῷ πλήθοντι ἐοικὼς
χειμάρρῳ, ὅς τ’ ὦκα ῥέων ἐκέδασσε γεφύρας·
sentences.l:
For he rushed across the plain, to a river in spate likened,
a winter-flowing one, which swiftly flowing scattered the bridges;
sentences.i: For he rushed across the plain like a river in flood, a winter torrent that in its swift course scatters the bridges;
sentences.n: A simile begins here. θῦνε is ‘rushed’ (θύνω, unaugmented imperfect), ἂμ πεδίον is ‘across the plain’ (ἂμ is ἀνά before π), and ποταμῷ πλήθοντι ἐοικώς is ‘like a river in spate’, ἐοικώς the perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’, with the dative; πλήθοντι ‘brimming’ is from πλήθω ‘be full’. χειμάρρῳ is the dative of χείμαρρος ‘winter-flowing’, a torrent fed by winter rain. ὅς τ’ is the relative with the epic τε of a general truth, and ἐκέδασσε is a gnomic aorist, a timeless ‘scatters’, which is why the English is in the present.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ οὔτ’ ἄρ τε γέφυραι ἐεργμέναι ἰσχανόωσιν,
οὔτ’ ἄρα ἕρκεα ἴσχει ἀλωάων ἐριθηλέων
ἐλθόντ’ ἐξαπίνης ὅτ’ ἐπιβρίσῃ Διὸς ὄμβρος·
sentences.i: neither the hemmed-in bridges hold it back nor the fences of the flourishing orchards check it, when it comes on suddenly, when the rain of Zeus bears down heavily;
sentences.n: τὸν is the river (the article as a pronoun, ‘it’), and οὔτ’ … οὔτ’ ἄρα … ‘neither … nor …’ gives the two things that fail to stop it. γέφυραι ἐεργμέναι is ‘bridges hemmed in’ (ἐεργμέναι is the perfect passive participle of εἴργω ‘shut in’), and the picture, bridges shut in by their banks or approaches, is the usual reading and not certain. ἰσχανόωσιν is the uncontracted form of ἰσχανάω ‘hold back’, and ἴσχει (ἴσχω) ‘check’; ἕρκεα ἀλωάων ἐριθηλέων is ‘the fences of the flourishing orchards’ (ἀλωή is a cultivated, fenced plot, ἐριθηλής ‘very flourishing’). ἐλθόντ’ is the accusative participle, ‘it coming’, ἐξαπίνης ‘suddenly’, and ἐπιβρίσῃ the aorist subjunctive of ἐπιβρίθω ‘bear down’; Διὸς ὄμβρος is ‘the rain of Zeus’.

sentences.t: πολλὰ δ’ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ ἔργα κατήριπε κάλ’ αἰζηῶν·
sentences.l: and many fine works of vigorous young men crashed down beneath it;
sentences.i: and many fine works of strong young men crash down beneath it;
sentences.n: πολλὰ … ἔργα … κάλ’ is ‘many fine works’ (κάλ’ is καλά elided), ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ ‘under it’, and κατήριπε the aorist of κατερείπω ‘crash down’. αἰζηῶν is the genitive plural of αἰζηός ‘vigorous young man’, the farmers whose work the flood destroys. The aorist is gnomic, as in ἐκέδασσε above, so the second layer uses the present.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὑπὸ Τυδεΐδῃ πυκιναὶ κλονέοντο φάλαγγες
Τρώων, οὐδ’ ἄρα μιν μίμνον πολέες περ ἐόντες.
sentences.l:
So under Tydeus’-son the thick battle-lines
of the Trojans were thrown into confusion, and did not stand against him, though many they were.
sentences.i: So before the son of Tydeus the thick battle-lines of the Trojans were thrown into confusion, and for all their numbers they did not stand against him.
sentences.n: ὣς … is the ‘so’ that closes the simile and brings it back to Diomedes: ὑπὸ Τυδεΐδῃ is ‘under Tydeus’-son’, i.e. at his hands, with the dative, and πυκιναὶ … φάλαγγες ‘the thick battle-lines’ is the subject of κλονέοντο ‘were thrown into confusion’. μίμνον is ‘stood against’ (the imperfect of μίμνω, a form of μένω), and πολέες περ ἐόντες ‘though being many’ (πολέες = πολλοί, περ ‘though’).

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησε Λυκάονος ἀγλαὸς υἱὸς
θύνοντ’ ἂμ πεδίον πρὸ ἕθεν κλονέοντα φάλαγγας,
αἶψ’ ἐπὶ Τυδεΐδῃ ἐτιταίνετο καμπύλα τόξα,
sentences.l:
Him then as he noticed, Lycaon’s splendid son,
rushing over the plain before himself, throwing the battle-lines into confusion,
at once at Tydeus’-son he stretched the bent bow,
sentences.i: As soon as Lycaon’s splendid son noticed him rushing over the plain before him and throwing the battle-lines into confusion, he at once drew the bent bow against the son of Tydeus,
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησε is ‘him then as he noticed’ (ἐνόησε ‘noticed’), the same pattern as 3.21 (Menelaus) and 3.30 (Alexander), with Λυκάονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός ‘Lycaon’s splendid son’ as the subject; the Greek does not name him here. θύνοντ’ is the participle ‘rushing’ and κλονέοντα is a transitive use of κλονέω, ‘driving into confusion’; πρὸ ἕθεν is ‘before himself’. ἐτιταίνετο is the imperfect middle of τιταίνω ‘stretch’, ‘drew’ the bow for himself, and καμπύλα τόξα is ‘the bent bow’, plural in form for a single bow.

sentences.t:
καὶ βάλ’ ἐπαΐσσοντα τυχὼν κατὰ δεξιὸν ὦμον
θώρηκος γύαλον·
sentences.l:
and hit him as he sprang on, hitting true on the right shoulder
the hollow of the breastplate;
sentences.i: and as he sprang forward he hit him, striking true on the right shoulder, on the hollow of the breastplate;
sentences.n: βάλ’ is the unaugmented ἔβαλε ‘hit’, with ἐπαΐσσοντα ‘as he darted forward’ the participle for Diomedes. τυχών is the aorist participle of τυγχάνω, ‘hitting the mark’, and κατὰ δεξιὸν ὦμον is ‘on the right shoulder’. θώρηκος γύαλον is ‘the hollow of the breastplate’: γύαλον ‘hollow’ is the curved plate, and the phrase says where on the shoulder the arrow found him.

sentences.t:
διὰ δ’ ἔπτατο πικρὸς ὀϊστός,
ἀντικρὺ δὲ διέσχε, παλάσσετο δ’ αἵματι θώρηξ.
sentences.l:
and through flew the bitter arrow,
and straight through it passed, and the breastplate was spattered with blood.
sentences.i: and the bitter arrow flew through, and went straight through, and the breastplate was spattered with blood.
sentences.n: διὰ δ’ ἔπτατο is ‘and through it flew’, with διά as an adverb (tmesis; ἔπτατο is the aorist middle of πέτομαι ‘fly’), and πικρὸς ὀϊστός is ‘the bitter arrow’; the diaeresis in ὀϊστός shows the ο and ι are sounded apart. ἀντικρὺ … διέσχε is ‘straight through it passed’ (διέχω), and παλάσσετο is the imperfect passive of παλάσσω ‘spatter’, ‘was spattered’, with αἵματι ‘with blood’; θώρηξ is ‘breastplate’.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἐπὶ μακρὸν ἄϋσε Λυκάονος ἀγλαὸς υἱός·
sentences.l: and over him shouted loudly Lycaon’s splendid son:
sentences.i: and over him Lycaon’s splendid son cried out loudly:
sentences.n: τῷ δ’ ἐπί is ‘and over him’, and μακρὸν ἄϋσε ‘shouted loudly’ is a stock phrase, with μακρόν as an adverb ‘long, loud’ and ἄϋσε an unaugmented aorist. The shout is a boast over a man he thinks he has hit mortally, and the next four lines are what he cries.

sentences.t:
ὄρνυσθε Τρῶες μεγάθυμοι κέντορες ἵππων·
βέβληται γὰρ ἄριστος Ἀχαιῶν, οὐδέ ἕ φημι
δήθ’ ἀνσχήσεσθαι κρατερὸν βέλος, εἰ ἐτεόν με
ὦρσεν ἄναξ Διὸς υἱὸς ἀπορνύμενον Λυκίηθεν.
sentences.l:
“Rouse yourselves, Trojans, great-hearted, goaders of horses;
for struck is the best of the Achaeans, and I do not think
that he will long endure the strong shaft, if truly
the lord, the son of Zeus, roused me, setting out from Lycia.”
sentences.i: “Rouse yourselves, great-hearted Trojans, goaders of horses: the best of the Achaeans has been struck, and I do not think he will long endure the strong shaft, if it was truly the lord, the son of Zeus, who sent me on my way when I set out from Lycia.”
sentences.n: ὄρνυσθε is the middle imperative of ὄρνυμι, ‘rouse yourselves’, addressed to Τρῶες μεγάθυμοι κέντορες ἵππων ‘great-hearted Trojans, goaders of horses’ (κέντωρ from κεντέω ‘goad’). βέβληται is the perfect passive of βάλλω ‘has been hit’, and οὐδέ ἕ φημι … ἀνσχήσεσθαι is ‘and I say of him that he will not endure’, that is, ‘I do not think he will endure’ (ἕ ‘him’, ἀνσχήσεσθαι the future infinitive of ἀνέχομαι ‘hold out, endure’, δήθ’ ‘long’), with κρατερὸν βέλος ‘the strong shaft’. εἰ ἐτεόν is ‘if truly’, and ἄναξ Διὸς υἱός is ‘the lord, son of Zeus’, a god the Greek does not name (the speaker can only mean the god who sent him, usually taken to be Apollo); ὦρσεν is the aorist of ὄρνυμι, ‘roused’, and ἀπορνύμενον ‘setting out’ agrees with με; Λυκίηθεν is ‘from Lycia’, with the ending -θεν.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος·
sentences.l: So he spoke, declaring;
sentences.i: So he declared aloud;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος is a formula that elsewhere ends a prayer, ‘So he spoke, praying’, because εὔχομαι means both ‘pray’ and ‘declare’; here it follows a loud claim, and the house rendering of εὔχομαι, ‘declare’, is kept. ἔφατ’ is ἔφατο, the elided past middle of φημί ‘say’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ οὐ βέλος ὠκὺ δάμασσεν,
ἀλλ’ ἀναχωρήσας πρόσθ’ ἵπποιιν καὶ ὄχεσφιν
ἔστη, καὶ Σθένελον προσέφη Καπανήϊον υἱόν·
sentences.l:
but him the swift shaft did not subdue,
but stepping back before the horses and the chariot
he stood, and addressed Sthenelus, Capaneus’ son:
sentences.i: but the swift shaft did not overcome him; stepping back, he stood before his horses and chariot and addressed Sthenelus, the son of Capaneus:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ is ‘but him’, Diomedes, and βέλος ὠκύ ‘swift shaft’ is the subject of οὐ … δάμασσεν, ‘did not subdue’ (δαμάζω). ἀναχωρήσας is the aorist participle ‘having drawn back’, and πρόσθ’ ἵπποιιν καὶ ὄχεσφιν ‘before the horses and the chariot’ uses the dual of ἵππος (the pair of horses) with ὄχεσφιν, the form in -φιν ‘chariot’. Σθένελον … Καπανήϊον υἱόν is ‘Sthenelus, Capaneus’ son’ (Καπανήϊος ‘of Capaneus’), his charioteer, and προσέφη is ‘addressed’.

sentences.t:
ὄρσο πέπον Καπανηϊάδη, καταβήσεο δίφρου,
ὄφρά μοι ἐξ ὤμοιο ἐρύσσῃς πικρὸν ὀϊστόν.
sentences.l:
“Up, good one, son of Capaneus, step down from the chariot,
that you may draw for me from my shoulder the bitter arrow.”
sentences.i: “Up, my good fellow, son of Capaneus, get down from the chariot, so that you may draw the bitter arrow out of my shoulder.”
sentences.n: ὄρσο is the aorist imperative middle of ὄρνυμι, ‘up! rouse yourself’, and πέπον is an affectionate address whose meaning is not known (taken as ‘good one’); Καπανηϊάδη is the vocative of the patronymic ‘son of Capaneus’. καταβήσεο is the aorist imperative middle of καταβαίνω, ‘step down’ (Attic κατάβηθι), with the genitive δίφρου ‘from the chariot’. ὄφρα with the subjunctive ἐρύσσῃς gives purpose, ‘so that you may draw’, with μοι ‘for me’ and ἐξ ὤμοιο ‘out of the shoulder’, and πικρὸν ὀϊστόν ‘the bitter arrow’ repeats line 99.
